text:
A bad database design rarely feels bad on day one. One table, every field in it, a few orders... and the first screen works. Ada's ordered twice, so her email's in there twice. Then she changes it. A rushed update fixes order one-oh-one... and misses the other. Now the database says, with total confidence, that one person has two emails.

And nothing in that update was illegal. Postgres did exactly what it was told. The problem is the design. Ada's email stopped being one fact and became copies, and every program has to keep them in step... by hand, forever. That's called an update anomaly. And you can rewrite code tomorrow... but data outlives code. So what is design, then?

It's answering the hard questions before your software answers them for you, inconsistently. Which things become tables? Which facts become columns? Which rows need an identity? Which tables point to which? And which values must be present, unique, or limited? SQL is just how you write the answers down. It isn't the design.

[curious] Take a library. Is a book the title in the catalog... or the copy on the shelf? Three copies of one title each have their own barcode, and get lent out separately. So a loan points at a copy, not a title. No SQL manual can tell you that. It's about what your system MEANS. And answers like that pay off later.

Say someone asks, which customers bought a notebook? With customers, orders, order items and products in their own tables, it's a short walk along links the design already drew. One name comes back. Ada Lovelace. Store each order as a sentence, Ada bought two notebooks and five pens, and that question becomes a project.
